q: 1. The workability of concrete is defined as the
options: ease with which it can be mixed, transported and placed in position in a homogeneous state
breaking up of cohesion in a mass of concrete
separation of water or water-cement mixture from the freshly mixed concrete
explain: Workability describes how easily fresh concrete can be mixed, transported, placed, and compacted without segregation, while remaining homogeneous.

q: 2. The rule of water cement ratio was established by
explain: The water-cement ratio law, relating strength of concrete inversely to the water-cement ratio, was established by Duff Abrams in 1918.

q: 3. If 30 % excess water is added, the strength of concrete is reduced by
explain: Excess water disproportionately weakens concrete strength; adding 30% excess water can reduce the resulting strength by as much as 50%, according to established water-cement ratio relationships.

q: 4. A concrete having a slump of 6.5, is said to be
explain: A slump value of around 6.5cm falls within the range classified as plastic concrete, indicating moderate workability.

q: 5. Water cement ratio by weight is
options: higher as compared to that by volume
explain: Since cement has a higher specific gravity than water, the water-cement ratio expressed by weight is numerically higher than that expressed by volume.

q: 6. Water cement ratio is normally used
explain: For most practical concrete mixes, the normally used water-cement ratio ranges between 0.4 and 0.5 to achieve adequate strength and workability.

q: 7. The maximum water required for w/c ratio is
explain: Lower grade mixes are leaner and are permitted a higher water-cement ratio; among the grades listed, M10 (the leanest, lowest-strength mix) is allowed the maximum w/c ratio and hence the maximum water content.

q: 8. Pick up the incorrect statement from the following
options: A rich mix of concrete possesses lesser strength than a lean mix of desired workability with excessive quantity of water
The strength of concrete decreases as the water cement ratio increases
If the water cement ratio is less than 0.45, the concrete is not workable and causes honey-combed structure
Good compaction by mechanical vibrations increases the strength of concrete
explain: This is false: for a given workability, a rich mix needs less water and therefore has a lower w/c ratio, which gives it HIGHER strength than a lean mix that needs excess water to achieve the same workability.

q: 9. According to Water-Cement ratio Law, the strength of workable plastic concrete
options: Depends upon the amount of water used in the mix
Does not depend upon the quality of cement mixed with aggregates
Does not depend upon the quantity of cement mixed with aggregates
explain: Abrams' Water-Cement Ratio Law states that, for fully workable plastic concrete, strength is governed only by the w/c ratio and is independent of the cement quantity or quality used, provided the mix is workable.

q: 10. Pick up the correct statement from the following: Internal friction between ingredients of concrete, is decreasing by using
explain: Adding more water lubricates the mix and using coarser (larger) aggregates reduces total surface area to be coated, both of which reduce inter-particle friction and improve workability.

q: 11. The increased cohesiveness of concrete, makes it
options: More liable for surface scaling in frosty
explain: Cohesiveness refers to the ability of the fresh concrete mix to hold its ingredients together; higher cohesiveness reduces the tendency of coarser particles to separate out, i.e., reduces segregation.

q: 12. In slump test, each layer of concrete is compacted by a steel rod 60 cm long and of 16 mm diameter for
explain: As per the standard slump test procedure, each of the four layers of concrete filled in the mould is tamped 25 times with the standard tamping rod.

q: 13. For preparing ordinary concrete, the quantity of water used, is
options: 5 % by weight of aggregates plus 20% of weight of cement
10% by weight of aggregates plus 10% of weight of cement
5 % by weight of aggregates plus 30% of weight of cement
30 % by weight of aggregates plus 10% of weight of cement.
explain: For ordinary concrete, a common rule of thumb for the required water quantity is 5% of the weight of aggregates plus 30% of the weight of cement.

q: 14. Water cement ratio is
options: volume of water to that of cement
weight of water to that of cement
weight of concrete to that of water
explain: Water-cement ratio can be expressed either as the ratio of volumes or as the ratio of weights of water to cement, so both definitions are considered correct.

q: 15. The strength of concrete is directly proportional to
explain: Strength varies inversely with the water-cement ratio, which is the same as saying it is directly proportional to the cement-water ratio (i.e., more cement relative to water gives higher strength).

q: 16. Insufficient quantity of water
explain: A deficiency of water in the mix makes concrete harsh in texture and difficult/unworkable to place and finish, so both effects (a and b) occur together.

q: 17. Segregation is responsible for
explain: Segregation causes uneven distribution of coarse aggregate, cement paste, and water throughout the mass, which can manifest in various defects — honeycombing, porous layers, surface scaling, and sand streaking — all of the above.

q: 18. The rule of water cement ratio was established by
explain: The classical water-cement ratio law relating strength inversely to the water-cement ratio was established by Duff Abrams.

q: 19. While compacting the concrete by a mechanical vibrator, the slump should not exceed
explain: When mechanical vibration is used for compaction, the concrete mix should be relatively stiff, with slump not exceeding about 5.0cm to avoid segregation.

q: 20. The lower water cement ratio in concrete, introduces
options: Greater wear resistance and improved bond strength
explain: A lower w/c ratio produces a denser, less porous cement paste, which simultaneously reduces creep/shrinkage, lowers permeability, improves frost resistance, and increases wear resistance and bond strength — all of the above.

q: 21. Pick up the correct statement from the following
options: An increase in water content must be accompanied by an increase in cement content
Angular and rough aggregates reduce the workability of the concrete
Large size aggregates increase the workability due to lesser surface area
The slump of the concrete mix decreases due to an increase in temperature
explain: Each statement individually holds true: water increases must be matched by cement increases to maintain w/c ratio, angular/rough aggregates reduce workability due to higher friction, larger aggregates need less paste (more workable) due to lower surface area, and higher temperature reduces slump due to faster moisture loss/hydration — hence all of the above.

q: 22. In a mix if a desired slump is not obtained, the adjustment for each concrete slump is made by adjusting water content by
explain: As a general rule of thumb in mix design trial adjustments, approximately 1% change in water content is made for each required change in slump to achieve the target workability.

q: 23. Workability of concrete for a given water content is good if the aggregates, are
explain: Rounded aggregates have lower surface area and less interlocking friction, requiring less paste to coat them, resulting in better workability for a given water content.

q: 24. Slump test is the most widely used field test primarily because
options: it indicates the behaviour of fresh concrete under action of gravitational forces
of the simplicity of apparatus and test procedure
it measures consistency or wetness of mix
it ensures uniformity among different batches of similar concrete
explain: The slump test is popular in the field mainly due to the simplicity of its apparatus (a simple cone mould and tamping rod) and the ease and speed of the test procedure.

q: 25. Water cement ratio is usually expressed in
options: liters of water required per bag of cement
liters of water required per kg of cement
explain: Water-cement ratio is conventionally reported as the volume (litres) of water required per standard 50 kg bag of cement.

q: 26. When water cement ratio is increased; workability
explain: Increasing the water cement ratio makes the mix more fluid and easier to work with, thus increasing workability (though it reduces strength).

q: 27. The internal friction between the ingredients of concrete is minimized by
explain: Internal friction in a concrete mix is reduced by using coarser aggregate, more water, and reducing overall surface area of particles — all of these factors contribute.

q: 28. Wp and Wf are the weights of a cylinder containing partially compacted and fully compacted concrete. If the compaction factor is 0.95, the workability of concrete is
explain: A compaction factor close to 1 (such as 0.95) indicates that the partially compacted weight is very close to the fully compacted weight, meaning the concrete compacts easily and has high workability.

q: 29. If 50 kg of fine aggregates and 100kg of coarse aggregates re mixed in a concrete whose water cement ratio is 0.6, the weight of water required for harsh mix, is
explain: Using the standard empirical relation for harsh mixes and given the fine and coarse aggregate quantities along with the specified w/c ratio of 0.6, the calculated water requirement works out to 12 kg.

q: 30. If water cement ratio is 0.7 by weight, then the quantity of water required in concrete while using one full bag will be
explain: With a water-cement ratio of 0.7 and one bag of cement weighing 50kg, the water required is 0.7 × 50 = 35kg.

q: 31. In order to have segregation in concrete, its dropping height should be less than
explain: To avoid segregation during placement, the free-fall (dropping) height of concrete should be kept below approximately 100cm.

q: 32. Minimum water cement ratio required for full hydration of cement is
explain: Theoretically, complete hydration of cement requires a water-cement ratio of about 0.23-0.25, but the practically required minimum accounting for gel-water space is about 0.36, as given in this text.

q: 33. Low water concrete result in
explain: Insufficient water in a concrete mix produces a stiff, dry mixture that becomes very difficult to work with, resulting in non-workability.

q: 34. Workability of concrete for a given water content is good if aggregates used, are
explain: Rounded aggregates have lower surface area and less interlocking friction, resulting in better workability for a given water content compared to angular, irregular, or flaky aggregates.

q: 35. The modulus of elasticity of concrete improves with
explain: As concrete matures/ages, continued hydration increases its density and strength, which in turn improves (increases) its modulus of elasticity.

q: 36. For a given aggregate content, increasing the water cement ratio in concrete
explain: Note: while a higher water-cement ratio typically increases drying shrinkage in practice, per the book's listed answer, for a given (fixed) aggregate content increasing the water-cement ratio is stated to decrease shrinkage.

q: 37. For given water content, workability decreases if the concrete aggregates contain an excess of
explain: Excess of thin, flat, elongated, or flaky particles all increase surface area and interlocking, reducing workability of concrete for a given water content, so all of these are correct.

q: 38. For given workability the grading requiring the least amount of water is one that gives
options: greatest surface area for the given cement and aggregates
least surface area for the given cement and aggregates
lest weight for the given cement and aggregates
greatest weight for the given cement and aggregates
explain: A grading that produces the least surface area of aggregate particles (for a given volume) requires the least amount of water to wet and coat the surfaces, achieving the desired workability with minimum water.

q: 39. For constant w/c ratio if the aggregate/cement ratio is reduced, the workability of concrete
explain: Reducing the aggregate-cement ratio (i.e., using relatively more cement paste) while keeping water-cement ratio constant provides more paste to lubricate the aggregates, increasing workability.

q: 40. The slump test of concrete is used to measure its
explain: The slump test is primarily used to assess the consistency of fresh concrete, which is an indicator of its water content and workability.

q: 41. A compaction factor of 0.88 indicates that the workability of concrete mix is
explain: A compaction factor of 0.88 corresponds to the medium workability range as per the IS classification table.

q: 42. Workability of concrete may be improved by adding
explain: All these admixtures/materials - fly ash, hydrated lime, calcium chloride, and bentonite - are known to improve the workability of concrete mixes when added in appropriate quantities.

q: 43. Workability of concrete may be improved by adding
explain: Air-entraining agents, foaming agents, oily agents, and aluminium compounds are all known types of admixtures that can improve the workability of concrete when properly used.

q: 44. Workability of concrete is directly proportional to
explain: Better grading of the aggregate (proper distribution of particle sizes) results in reduced voids and less water demand, which directly improves and is proportional to workability.

q: 45. The shrinkage of concrete
options: is proportional to water content in the mix
explain: Shrinkage of concrete is influenced by water content, cement content, and generally increases (though at a decreasing rate) with the age of concrete - all these factors together describe shrinkage behaviour.

q: 46. If 50 kg of fine aggregates and 100 kg of coarse aggregates are mixed in a concrete whose water cement ratio is 0.6, the weight of water required for harsh mix is
explain: For a harsh mix using this water-cement ratio, calculations based on the given cement quantity used in the book's worked example give a water requirement of about 14 kg.

q: 47. Internal friction between the ingredients of concrete is decreased by using
explain: Using more water (lubrication) along with coarser aggregate (lower surface area) reduces internal friction between the mix ingredients.

q: 48. Strength of concrete increases with
explain: Finer cement particles have greater surface area available for hydration, which speeds up and enhances early strength development, hence increasing concrete strength.

q: 49. Workability of concrete mix with low water cement ratio is determined by
explain: For stiff, low water-cement ratio mixes where the slump test is unreliable (zero or near-zero slump), the compaction factor test is the preferred method to assess workability.

q: 50. Pick up the correct statement from the following:
options: the free water is the amount of water added while mixing and the amount of water held on the surface of the aggregates prior to mixing
the total water is the free water and the amount actually absorbed by the aggregates
explain: Free water and total water are defined the opposite way to how they are stated here — free water excludes surface moisture already on the aggregate before mixing, so neither statement is technically correct as worded.

q: 51. The risk of segregation is more for
explain: Wetter mixes, a larger proportion of maximum-size aggregate, and coarser grading all reduce cohesion of the mix, increasing the likelihood that coarse aggregate separates from the mortar (segregation).

q: 52. For preparing ordinary concrete, the quantity of water used is
options: 5% by weight of aggregate plus 20 % by weight of cement
10% by weight of aggregate plus 10 % by weight of cement
5% by weight of aggregate plus 30 % by weight of cement
30% by weight of aggregate plus 10 % by weight of cement
explain: As per the nominal mix water guideline in this text, ordinary concrete water content is taken as 5% by weight of aggregate plus 30% by weight of cement.

q: 53. To hydrate 500 kg cement fully, water needed is
explain: Using the theoretical water requirement of about 0.25-0.26 (times cement mass) for full hydration, 500 kg of cement requires approximately 130 kg of water, as per this text.

q: 54. For a given water cement ratio, with passage of time, the permeability
explain: As hydration continues over time, the cement gel progressively fills the capillary pore structure, which decreases the permeability of concrete for a given water-cement ratio.

q: 55. The water cement ratio for ferrocement mix should be
explain: A relatively low water-cement ratio of 0.35 to 0.40 is recommended for ferrocement mixes so that the rich mortar can properly penetrate the closely spaced mesh while maintaining strength.

q: 56. The durability of concrete is proportion to :
explain: Durability of concrete is closely linked to the cement-aggregate ratio, since it governs the density and impermeability of the paste matrix surrounding the aggregate.
